lawyer:
Fazlul Huq, AAG ----- For the Appellant. 
SK Sinha, Advocate ----- For the Respondents.
parties:
Bangladesh ----- Appellant
Vs.
Dewan Obaidur Reza Chowdhury and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
"Where the subject-matter of the suit is immovable property, the plaint shall contain a description of the property sufficient to identify it, and, in case such property can be identified by boundaries or numbers in a record of settlement of survey, the plaint shall specify such boundaries". From the above it is clear that the description of the suit-land can also be given by boundaries for proper identification of the same and the Court may be satisfied with the same. In the instant case the trial Court possibly without noticing the above provision of law and the description of the suitland by boundaries wrongly held that the subject matter of the suit was not identifiable. The lower Appellate Court however took the correct view and rightly reversed the finding of the trial Court. Apart from that, the instant suit was a suit for declaration of title only and in fact for correction of the alleged wrong record of right in the Khatian and there was neither any prayer for confirmation of his possession nor recovery of possession of the suit and. From that point of view also it appears that the point of alleged vagueness was not so material for the adjudication of the present suit. So, I find no substance in the contention of the learned Advocate for the appellant in his first point. The next contention of the teamed Advocate for the appellant is that the impugned judgment is not a proper judgment of reversal as the lower Appellate Court has failed to advert to the reasoning of the trial Court in deciding the suit and also it has failed to take into consideration the material evidence particularly the documentary evidence of the contesting defendant, as a result there has been a serious miscarriage of justice. In support of his contention, the learned Advocate for the appellant has referred to a number of decisions reported in 35 DLR AD page 216 and 17 DLR pages 687, 547, 541 and 105. In elaborating his submission, the learned Advocate for the appellant has drawn my attention to the judgment of the trial Court as well as to that of the court of appeal below and also to the evidence on record. It has already been stated that both the sides adduced evidence, oral and documentary in support of their respective cases. From the side of the defendant appellant a number of documents were filed and they were marked as Ext. A to G(2); to these documents, the trial Court took into consideration, most of them along with the documents filed by the plaintiff and decided the question of title and possession of the parties over the suit lands, but it appears from the judgment of the lower Appellate Court that save and except document Ext. E of the contesting defendant, the learned Subordinate Judge has not taken into consideration any other documents of the defendant, but those documents appear to be quite material not only to support the defence case but also to test the genuineness of the plaintiffs document  of title particularly Ext. 1. Apart from that, it appears that the trial Court made some observation with regard to the question of adverse possession. But the lower Appellate Court is silent on the same. Besides, it is also the contention of the learned Advocate for the appellant that the lower appellate Court on a misreading and also upon material mistaken assumption of fact came to an illegal finding in respect of the right, title of the plaintiff. It appears from the judgment of the trial Court that it held while considering the question of possession as follows : "PW 4 Tozammul Ali has corroborated the evidence adduced by PWs 1, 2 and 3, I do not find any contradiction in their evidence. I therefore, accept their evidence and opine that the plaintiff has possession in the suit land. "But the lower appellate Court appears to have held apparently upon misreading and also mistaken assumption of fact that "PW 4 Tajammul Ali deposed in corroboration of the plaint case of settlement and possession of the disputed land by plaintiff". The lower Court found that there was no contradiction amongst the PWs in respect of plaintiff's case of settlement and possession. It is apparent that the trial Court in its observation did not refer to any settlement. In the observation of the lower appellate Court the word "settlement" was wrongly quoted. From the above, it appears that the lower appellate Court did not apply its judicial mind to the facts and circumstances of the case and the materials on record and arbitrarily found the mere submission of the learned Advocate for the plaintiff to be a view taken by the trial Court in respect of the alleged tenancy right of the plaintiff which is not correct. In the trial Court's judgment it has been observed by the learned Munsif as follows:— "The learned Advocate for the plaintiff has argued that he had called for all papers relating to the. suit land from the ex-landlord. The non-production of those documents by the defendant would lead us to presume that the plaintiff has tenancy right in the suit-land. The above fact by itself does not exonerate the plaintiff from proving ' his case. "The plaintiff in order to succeed must prove, beyond reasonable amount of doubt his title in the suit land." 

 10. But with regard to this, the lower appellate Court observed as follows" "In this connection, it is to be noted that the plaintiff called for all necessary papers to prove his jote right from the ex-landlord. It was argued by the learned lawyer for the plaintiff that he called for all papers relating to disputed lands from the ex-landlord but none were produced and the non production of these documents by the defendants would lead us to presume that the plaintiffs had tenancy right in the suit land, observed by the learned lower Court." The learned Subordinate Judge without noticing the subsequent line of observation of the learned Munsif, it appears that he took the alleged presumption of the tenancy right of the plaintiff in the suit land as urged by the learned Advocate for the plaintiff to be an acceptance of the said right by the trial Court. Thus from an analysis of the facts and circumsatnces of the case and the materials on records I am of the opinion that the judgment of the Court of appeal below is not a proper judgment of reversal anal the same should be set aside. In view of the above, on setting aside the impugned judgment and decree, the appeal is generally sent back on remand to the Court of appeal below for rehearing and fresh decision in accordance with law, but as it is a very old suit of the year 1966 and when all materials are available on record, I feel that in the interest of justice this Court should exercise its jurisdiction under section 103 of the Code of Civil Procedure and decide the issues involved in the suit or the appeal on consideration of the materials on record. And this view of mine finds support from the decisions in the case of Khandakar Mohiuddin Vs. Syed Moin Ahmed reported in 28 DLR SC 85 and in the case Ajufannessa @ Aji Bibi and others Vs. Safar Miah and ors. reported in 30 DLR (SC) 41 and also in the case of Md. Altafur Rahman Vs. Tantijur Rahman reported in 30 DLR (SC) 236. In that view of the matter, I therefore want to decide the appeal afresh on consideration of the evidence on record and the facts and circumstances of the case.
